features.title: Tracked hands become interaction events
features.body: I connected tracked-hand input to the actions available inside the experience. Touch, pinch, and grab are meaningful because they can change an encounter, rather than simply animate a virtual hand. The important implementation boundary is the transition from a recognized hand action to the response of a specific scene object.
features.inspect: The hand-input component, its event binding, and the receiving object or script.
features.demo: Perform one gesture slowly and show the corresponding event and visible response together.

features.title: Interaction changes the scene and its materials
features.body: I connected the interaction to runtime scene and material states. The visual response is part of the participant's action: a figure or the surrounding encounter changes when the action is accepted. This separates the availability of an input from the consequence that gives it meaning.
features.inspect: The affected object and material beside the component that changes their state.
features.demo: Show the same object before, during, and after one accepted interaction.

features.title: A different role requires different available actions
features.body: NARCI places the participant in a confined encounter, while Be NARCI gives them actions that affect other human-like figures. I built the Unity XR encounters around that change of role. Spatial restriction, the reachable objects, and the resulting responses carry the concept alongside the spoken content.
features.inspect: The two scene setups and the objects that receive participant input in each.
features.demo: Record each experience separately so their different interaction rules remain visible.

features.title: The NPC conversation belongs to the puzzle
features.body: I integrated a GPT-based NPC into the Unity VR game. Players try to obtain a protected password or useful clue through conversation. The language interaction therefore has an explicit gameplay purpose: information from the encounter can help the player satisfy an escape condition.
features.inspect: The conversation component, a submitted turn, and the response presented by the NPC.
features.demo: Compare an ordinary question with an attempt that produces useful puzzle information.

features.title: Information is connected to progression
features.tools: Puzzle state · gameplay conditions · world feedback
features.body: I connected the dialogue encounter to puzzle and progression conditions. A reply is one part of a larger game loop that also includes the player's actions and the world's response. The original progression condition still needs a focused source capture. The independent code example below demonstrates a separate, inspectable approach to authorizing progression.
features.inspect: The actual progression condition and the scene object changed when it succeeds.
features.demo: Keep the clue, the player's follow-up action, and the resulting world change in one recording.

features.title: Jailbreaking becomes a playable constraint
features.tools: NPC behavior · interaction design · scene flow
features.body: I built the VR experience around the tension between a character's constraints and the player's attempts to work around them. The premise is a fictional escape-game mechanic. Escape Metro and RedFlight AI are two names for this same project, rather than separate AI systems or model-security studies.
features.inspect: The character's authored constraint and the game situation in which it matters.
features.demo: Show how one conversation changes the player's next available action in the environment.

features.title: Data becomes a family of generated forms
features.body: I contributed to the collaborative translation of periodic-table data into harmonograph-based forms. The central decision is the mapping: a structured difference in the source becomes a visible difference in the generated form. The original data-to-parameter contract should accompany any future code or equation presented as the production implementation.
features.inspect: One source entry, its actual generation parameters, and the resulting object.
features.demo: Compare two elements while keeping the visualization rule consistent.

features.title: Generated objects become spatial relationships
features.body: I helped construct the Unity world that organizes those forms into a speculative universe. The work does more than display isolated objects. Arrangement, scale, and relationships create an environment in which the data can be encountered as a larger visual system.
features.inspect: The generated forms in the Unity scene and their organization into a larger environment.
features.demo: Move from a single form to the surrounding group without changing its identity.

features.title: The viewer enters the translation
features.body: The project makes its visual system inhabitable through VR. My contribution combines the translation method with building the virtual world. The experience asks how a classification can become a place, rather than claiming that the world is a physically accurate simulation of atoms or chemical behavior.
features.inspect: The VR viewing setup and the scene as experienced from the participant's position.
features.demo: Record navigation from one generated form to its surrounding spatial relationships.

features.title: A spatial action produces a spray effect
features.body: I implemented the Unity VR spray interaction and its particle feedback. The spray makes the action legible while it happens: the participant can see the direction and spread of the mark-making gesture. That short-lived feedback has a different job from the painted surface that remains afterward.
features.inspect: The input binding, particle emission, and the surface-contact information used by the painting path.
features.demo: Start and stop the spray while keeping the wall and input visible.

features.title: The wall stores the result in a render target
features.body: I used a dynamic RenderTexture in the wall material so paint could accumulate on the virtual surface. Surface-hit information connects the spray to that texture state. The precise hit-to-texture-coordinate path still needs the original code or a close Editor recording, rather than an invented raycast or collision implementation.
features.inspect: The RenderTexture asset or runtime target and the wall material that reads it.
features.demo: Show the render target updating, then stop the particles and show the mark that remains.

features.title: A virtual subway becomes a space to alter
features.body: I built the painting interaction within a virtual subway setting. Moving the act into VR changes its relationship to permission and physical residue. The technical result is an environment the participant can visibly alter. Disk persistence, save/load, and environmental benefit are separate claims and are not assumed here.
features.inspect: The paintable surfaces and their relationship to the participant's reachable space.
features.demo: Paint across the actual supported area and show how the surface carries the result.

features.title: Connect a participant's body to Unity
features.tools: Azure Kinect · body and depth input · C#
features.body: I connected Azure Kinect sensing to the Unity installation. The participant's body supplies live input for the encounter instead of acting only as a subject in a prerecorded video. The meaningful boundary is where sensor data becomes the participation event used by the application.
features.inspect: The actual sensor connection, body input, and the component that recognizes participation.
features.demo: Show a person entering the sensing area, performing the action, and producing the corresponding event.

features.title: Let live input enter an authored Timeline
features.tools: Unity Timeline · runtime events · media sequencing
features.body: I integrated sensor-driven interaction with Timeline-based presentation. Authored media has its own timing, while a participant acts at an unpredictable moment. The implementation brings those two timelines together so an input can lead into the memorial sequence and its screen transitions.
features.inspect: The Timeline asset, its bound media tracks, and the code or event that changes playback.
features.demo: Keep the participant, recognized event, Timeline playhead, and Game view visible during one transition.

features.title: Compose the memorial from a live presence
features.tools: Live silhouette · archival imagery · Unity composition
features.body: I integrated the live participant image with archival-image composition and the timed presentation. The resulting memorial image connects a present body with historical material. Sensing, the image composition, and the sequence remain separate parts of the technical explanation so each can be inspected.
features.inspect: The live input image, the composition stage, and its final presentation layer.
features.demo: Record the source body image and the memorial result together, followed by the actual reset behavior.

features.title: Bring Kinect v2 movement into Unity
features.body: I connected Kinect v2 body tracking to the Unity installation. This is the Kinect v2 work, separate from the Azure Kinect integration in To Eternity. The input represents a visitor's movement that can be connected to a character in the museum presentation.

features.title: Map a living body onto Kim Yuk
features.tools: Body mapping · character transform and animation
features.body: I connected the tracked visitor to the digital Kim Yuk character. The technical task is the mapping between the sensor's movement data and the figure's performance. Its purpose is immediate recognizability: a visitor should be able to connect their own action to the character's response.
features.inspect: The actual body-to-character mapping component, rig, and affected transforms.
features.demo: Perform a slow arm movement and a change in body position so the correspondence is easy to follow.

features.title: Present the mapping as an encounter
features.body: I integrated the interaction into a museum-facing presentation. The digital scholar becomes someone the visitor can move with, rather than a static model. The character's framing and the physical tracking area are part of how the interaction is understood.

features.title: Read movement as a live control
features.body: I used Kinect v2 to bring full-body movement into the Unity work. The body becomes a source of control data for a geometric environment. Tracking is the input stage, while the visual interpretation of the movement belongs to the artwork's own mapping.
features.inspect: The tracked-body data and the scene component that consumes it.

features.body: I mapped movement into geometric visual environments. The goal was an alternate visual body rather than a realistic avatar. The relation between a movement and a changing form needs to remain discoverable even when the visual world deliberately changes familiar spatial relationships.

features.title: Carry a live portrait through an AI pipeline
features.body: I integrated the portrait-processing pipeline across Unity, Barracuda, and Python/OpenCV. A visitor image moves into processing and returns as material for the final portrait. Model inference, input preparation, and the Unity presentation are separate responsibilities. The exact model architecture and preprocessing contract should be shown from the original project assets.

features.demo: Use one portrait to show the source image and each implemented processing result.

features.title: Combine style transformation with visual filters
features.body: I combined AI-based processing with visual filtering and portrait composition. The historical magazine appearance is produced by a sequence of operations, rather than every visible effect belonging to one model. The processed subject, framing, background, and graphic treatment have to work as one finished image.
features.inspect: The style-processing stage, filter controls, and final composed portrait.
features.demo: Toggle the actual available layers for the same image so their separate contributions are visible.

features.title: Move the result into a shared installation
features.body: I connected the portrait-making system to archival output and an external display, within an installation supporting up to four simultaneous participants. Network communication serves the exhibition workflow. The specific roles of TCP and UDP need the original configuration or source capture. This is not commercial online-game operations experience.
features.inspect: The actual participant routing, saved output, and sender/receiver components for the public display.
features.demo: Follow one completed portrait from its creation station to the gallery display, then show the actual multi-participant setup.

features.title: Control cloud form independently of object motion
features.body: I developed shaders for cloud-like forms and connected runtime control to their visual behavior. Internal flow and deformation are different controls from translating the object itself. The form can change while its Transform remains a separate part of the game logic. The independent C# and HLSL example below isolates that principle.
features.inspect: Transform values beside the actual shader parameters and their C# control path.
features.demo: Keep the object position fixed while reversing the internal flow or changing deformation strength.

features.title: Render droplet fusion through raymarched metaballs
features.body: I implemented raymarched metaballs for droplet-like forms that appear to merge continuously. The visible surface is produced from a field rather than simply intersecting rigid sphere meshes. Rendering a fused surface and determining gameplay contact remain separate responsibilities, so a convincing visual merge should not be mistaken for a matching physics collider.
features.inspect: The production field definition and raymarching pass beside the separate contact or proximity logic.
features.demo: Move two field sources together, show the fusion, and identify how interaction is evaluated.

features.title: Preserve the artist's control over transformation
features.tools: Authored growth targets · fixed topology · runtime control
features.body: The public technical archive also documents growth states prepared with consistent mesh topology. Corresponding vertices let authored forms belong to one transformation sequence. This gives the artist direct control over the intended silhouettes while C# and material controls connect the visual work to a running Unity scene.
features.inspect: The Maya target states, their shared topology, and their actual Unity control.
features.demo: Move through the authored states and distinguish that process from procedural shader deformation.
